A modern Korean syllable block begins wi: A modern Korean syllable block begins with an initial consonant (초성) and a vowel (중성). It may end with a final consonant (종성), commonly called batchim. The patterns are therefore CV or CVC. 가 contains ㄱ + ㅏ; 한 contains ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ.
A syllable pronounced without an audible: A syllable pronounced without an audible opening consonant still needs an initial position in writing. Korean uses ㅇ as a silent initial before a vowel: 아 is ㅇ + ㅏ, and 우 is ㅇ + ㅜ. In the final position, the same letter represents the /ng/ sound, as in 강.

Computers can represent modern Hangul sy: Computers can represent modern Hangul syllables as precomposed Unicode characters. Add K next, and a standard input method can reinterpret that ㄴ as the initial of a new syllable, giving 하나 from ㅎㅏㄴㅏ.
